title: Towards a Sustainable Indoor Lighting Design: Effects of Artificial Light on the Emotional State of Adolescents in the Classroom
research_question: To analyze the articles published on the non-visual effects of light, specifically LED luminaires and electronic screens, to elucidate the spectral composition and irradiance of new LED luminaires for use in homes and educational centers, and to consider the consequences of light emitted by laptops for teenagers, ultimately studying the different sources of artificial light adolescents may receive and the physiological and psychological consequences of their absorption.

participants.description: The review synthesizes findings related to human beings, specifically adolescents and children, in various settings (home, public spaces, educational centers).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: New LED luminaires for indoor lighting in homes and public spaces (educational centers), with varying spectral composition and intensity, including cold color temperatures (4000 K, 6500 K, 9000 K).
Screens of televisions, computer equipment, and mobile phones, emitting blue light.
Natural sunlight, daylight, and natural light-dark cycles.

findings.antecedent: Blue light emitted by electronic equipment (laptops, mobile phones, TVs)
findings.consequent: Irradiance level compared to solar irradiance
findings.quote: the amount of blue light emitted by electronic equipment is lower than that emitted by modern luminaires and thousands of times less than solar irradiance.

findings.antecedent: Small amounts of light received at night
findings.mechanism: Disruption of circadian rhythms and melatonin suppression.
findings.quote: latest research warns that these small amounts of light received at night can have pernicious non-visual effects on adolescents.

findings.antecedent: General indoor lighting via LED luminaires with cold color temperatures (4000 K, 6500 K, 9000 K)
findings.mechanism: Irradiance levels are never enough to cause damage if not looking at the naked light source.
findings.quote: general lighting levels used in interiors via LED luminaires with cold color temperatures... are never enough to cause damage to the retina, as long as one does not look at the naked light source.

findings.antecedent: Blue light emitted by electronic devices (LED lights, computers, mobile phones)
findings.consequent: Damage to the retinas of users (including teenagers)
findings.mechanism: Irradiance from these devices is 1000 to 10,000 times lower than solar irradiance, and experimental studies used much higher, monochromatic blue light levels on animal/cell cultures.
findings.quote: it is not considered plausible that this equipment is harmful to the retina, as our eyes can survive 1000 to 10,000 times more light than they receive from these devices from the sun.

findings.consequent: Alteration of natural cycles of sleep and wakefulness, reducing sleep hours
findings.quote: Artificial light has facilitated great advances in many fields, but it can also pose a risk as it can alter the natural cycles of sleep and wakefulness

findings.antecedent: Chronodisruption (alteration of internal temporal order of physiological, biological, and behavioral rhythms)
findings.consequent: Increased incidence of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, cognitive and emotional disorders, premature aging, and some cancers
findings.mechanism: Disruption of internal biological clocks and hormonal balance (e.g., melatonin, cortisol).
findings.quote: Epidemiological studies show that chronodisruption is associated with an increased incidence of metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, cognitive and emotional disorders

findings.antecedent: Minimum amount of light received from 9:00-10:00 p.m. (even as low as 1 lx)
findings.consequent: Delay in transition from serotonin to melatonin, delaying rest process
findings.quote: the minimum amount of light that we receive from 9:00-10:00 p.m. will delay the transition from serotonin to melatonin

findings.antecedent: Composition of light used for indoor lighting (especially blue light)
findings.consequent: Balance between serotonin and melatonin, influencing circadian cycles
findings.mechanism: Blue light absorption by ipRGCs, which are sensitive to light from UVA to red with a peak in blue, influencing melatonin elimination and serotonin replacement.
findings.quote: the composition of light used for indoor lighting can influence the balance between serotonin and melatonin and therefore, our circadian cycles.

findings.antecedent: Low indoor lighting and natural light exposure
findings.consequent: Increase in myopia among children and adolescents worldwide
findings.mechanism: Unknown, but suspected to be related to electronic device use and short time outdoors.
findings.quote: relate low indoor lighting and natural light to the increase in myopia among children and adolescents worldwide

findings.antecedent: Increased exposure to natural light (daylight) in classrooms
findings.consequent: Better reading and math test scores for students
findings.mechanism: Natural light positively affects human performance, concentration, and potentially reduces cognitive fatigue.
findings.quote: Students exposed to more natural light (i.e., daylight) in their classrooms perform better than students exposed to less natural light

findings.antecedent: Poor lighting (inadequate or excessive, non-uniform, glare-inducing) in classrooms
findings.consequent: Negative effects on children's performance and mood (e.g., headaches, impaired visual task performance, maladaptive behaviors)
findings.mechanism: Visual discomfort, reduced contrast, and potential cognitive load from poor lighting.
findings.quote: poor lighting, whether natural or artificial, has notable negative effects on children's performance and mood

findings.antecedent: Insufficient light levels in classrooms (e.g., no natural lighting, warm white 3000K vs cold white 5500K fluorescents)
findings.consequent: Inadequate levels of hormones (e.g., cortisol), leading to negative effects on children's behavior
findings.mechanism: Influence on pineal gland and biorhythms.
findings.quote: insufficient light levels with inadequate levels of hormones, leading to negative effects on children's behavior

findings.antecedent: Bright white light (more than 1000 lx) or light enriched in blue range
findings.consequent: Increased alertness, reduced drowsiness, increased vigilance, modulated cognitive functions (logical reasoning, creativity)
findings.mechanism: Activation effect, direct effect on serotonin metabolism.
moderators_reported: individual differences (PER3 gene, age, cognitive domain, task difficulty)
findings.quote: Bright white light can have an activation effect that is linked to increased alertness, reduced drowsiness, and increased levels of vigilance

findings.antecedent: Periods of exposure to bright light (more than 1000 lx) during the day
findings.mechanism: May be due to a direct effect of bright light on serotonin metabolism.
findings.quote: During the day, periods of exposure to bright light (more than 1000 lx) can lead to better social and emotional interaction.

findings.consequent: Increased risk of headache, dizziness, sleep problems, insomnia, dependence syndrome, mental or behavioral disorders (e.g., anxiety, psychopathological depression)
findings.mechanism: Physiological reasons such as increased nerve conductivity in children, and developing brains in adolescents.
findings.quote: The dependence and addiction due to the indiscriminate use of mobile phones by children and adolescents all over the world already have attention within the scientific community

findings.antecedent: Frequent use of electronic equipment during the day and night (especially in bed)
findings.consequent: Increased risk of short sleep duration, long sleep onset latency, and increased sleep deficits in adolescents
findings.mechanism: Light emitted by screens suppresses melatonin and disrupts circadian rhythms.
findings.quote: The use of electronic devices during the day and night was associated with an increased risk of a short sleep duration, a long sleep onset latency, and increased sleep deficits.

mechanisms: Disruption of circadian rhythms due to artificial light exposure at night.
Melatonin suppression and serotonin balance alteration by light, especially blue light.
Activation of alertness and cognitive functions by bright white/blue-enriched light.
Visual discomfort and cognitive load from poor lighting conditions.
Physiological effects of light on internal organs and hormone production (e.g., HPA axis, cortisol).
Developing brains of adolescents being more vulnerable to light effects and mobile phone dependence.
moderators: Age (children/adolescents vs. adults, prepubescent vs. postpubescent)
School district and student population characteristics (race, socioeconomic status)
Time of day and season of light exposure
implementation_implications: Develop a 'manual for the good use of electronic equipment by adolescents'.
Train professionals in charge of public building maintenance (schools) on correct acquisition and assembly of lights.
Inform public bodies responsible for consumer protection about blue light proportion in new luminaires.
Integrate photobiology content into health-related curricula from early stages.
Prioritize natural or artificial lighting according to natural parameters in new and existing educational centers.
Develop regulations to control light composition in new luminaires.
Increase exposure to sunlight to reduce health consequences of circadian disruption.
Implement ethical and healthy regulations related to lighting to optimize health and performance of young people in school contexts.
Design classrooms to maximize natural light while avoiding visual discomfort.
Consider dynamic lighting systems that vary light intensity and spectral content throughout the day and seasons.

limitations: Scarcity of existing research in this field (effects of continuously increasing or decreasing percentage of blue light in a systemic way on humans, especially children and adolescents).
Inability to control luminaires being made in real time (companies can buy LEDs, group them, use programming systems with remote control to change light composition).
Lack of legislation on non-visual effects of light, preventing legal limitation of blue light proportion.
No concrete recommendations can be given to safely improve the health of adolescents due to limitations.
Photobiology not existing as a separate subject, leading to fragmented research across disciplines.
No publications found on the composition of light in adolescent training centers or psychological responses to it.
Specific causes for the myopia pandemic remain unknown, and no article has provided conclusive results.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Towards a Sustainable Indoor Lighting Design: Effects of Artificial Light on the Emotional State of Adolescents in the Classroom
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In recent years, articles have been published on the non-visual effects of light, specifically the light emitted by the new luminaires with light emitting diodes (LEDs) and by the screens of televisions, computer equipment, and mobile phones. Professionals from the world of optometry have raised the possibility that the blue part of the visible light from sources that emit artificial light could have pernicious effects on the retina. The aim of this work is to analyze the articles published on this subject, and to use existing information to elucidate the spectral composition and irradiance of new LED luminaires for use in the home and in public spaces such as educational centers, as well as considering the consequences of the light emitted by laptops for teenagers. The results of this research show that the amount of blue light emitted by electronic equipment is lower than that emitted by modern luminaires and thousands of times less than solar irradiance. On the other hand, the latest research warns that these small amounts of light received at night can have pernicious non-visual effects on adolescents. The creation of new LED luminaires for interior lighting, including in educational centers, where the intensity of blue light can be increased without any specific legislation for its control, makes regulatory developments imperative due to the possible repercussions on adolescents with unknown and unpredictable consequences.
